Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Munitions and Supply arising out of a press dispatch from Washington appearing in this morning's paper. The dispatch states:
A production council to utilize to the limit the manufacturing facilities of Canada, Britain and the United States in fabricating the weapons required for the united nations on all fronts, will be set up here this week.
War Production

That is, in Washington. Would the minister tell the house whether or not that report is accurate. It then goes on to say:
Canada will not be represented directly on the production board, but its interests will be handled by Nelson.
That is Mr. Donald M. Nelson of the United States. Is this report accurate; and if 30, why is it that Canada is not being represented?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Munitions and Supply
subtopic: PRESS REPORT AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF COUNCIL TO UTILIZE FULLY UNITED NATIONS FACILITIES

Canada will not be represented directly on the production board, but its interests will be handled by Nelson.

speechtext:
If this is to keep up I suggest to the government that they impose closure. That was done before by Right Hon. R. B. Bennett when the circumstances were not quite the same. I urge upon the government that it adopt some means of removing this bane of democracy. Talking incessantly is one of the things that destroys democracy. Some toleration should be extended; we all believe in freedom of speech, but this excessive speech-making takes up the time of the house and wastes the money of the country. I am sure it is the opinion of 90 per cent of the members of this house that this action should be taken.

War Appropriation-War Services
While I am on my feet I should like to suggest to the committee one way by which some of this money might be obtained. The federal government should suggest to the provincial governments that they do away with the traffic in liquor. Two hundred million dollars in the form of planes and guns for the front would do more good than it does the way it is spent now, especially in the beer parlours for the ladies. I know this is not under your jurisdiction, but if the provinces are not ready to abolish this traffic, the federal government has it in its power to abolish liquor completely.

Yesterday I asked the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) for some information which should now be available. This has to do with a matter that concerns not only this house but the country as a whole-the results of the survey made by the government of the number of men available in the various age groups. As was mentioned last evening by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Boucher), the position to-day is that in certain districts men between the ages of twenty and twenty-four years are being called up, whereas in other districts the call has been extended up to the thirty-year-old group. The minister stated that so far as certain age groups are concerned, the point of exhaustion is being approached.
What I asked for yesterday-it was no fault of the minister that he did not then give an answer-was the number of men in the different districts between twenty-one and twenty-four years of age and between twenty-four and thirty years of age who are still available for war service. This information is in the possession of the government; for the minister was able to say that the number of men within certain groups is about exhausted, and also he admitted yesterday that the information is available on the basis of the national registration. I said as reported on page 2933 of Hansard:
The information must be available, on the basis of national registration, which will show exactly the number of young men in the various age classes and the records of the numbers who have been called up.
To which the minister replied, "Oh, yes." The country must have the information I am asking for in order to know the present position of our voluntary system of recruiting and the possibility of being able to secure the necessary men by the continuance of the
voluntary system. We would then be able to come to a conclusion as to whether or not the time has come to extend the age class beyond thirty years, possibly to thirty-five or thirty-eight for single men, as well as including married men. What was the nature of the survey made by the government? What has that survey shown? What pool of man-power is available for labour, as shown by the recent census? How many men are still available for service within the age groups twenty to twenty-four years and twenty-four to thirty years, according rto' divisions?
The calls being made to-day are made in a spasmodic, slipshod and unscientific manner. We are going into one part of the country and calling up men to the age of thirty years, while in another part of the country we are calling up men only to the age of twenty-four years. Surely the time has come when there should be equality in the calls. Unless we have this information, the debate on the necessity for changing our voluntary system to compulsory selective service will be based merely on individual impression. All we will have will be one man's against another man's opinion, neither of them based on statistical information.
Only yesterday we saw an example of the difference of opinion that can exist. The adjutant general gave certain figures which appeared in the press, in regard to the proportion of men called up as R recruits who ultimately find their way into the active army. At the same time and in the same paper there appeared a statement by the deputy minister of national war services which indicated different percentages. Surely the minister is in position to furnish the house and the country with the information I have asked for. Without this information each member will have to substitute his own opinion for facts based on statistics.

Mr. Chairman, I have already covered the ground in respect to which the hon. member for Lake Centre is asking for information in so far as it is possible to cover [DOT] it. I indicated that in one of the administrative divisions, Kingston, the point of exhaustion of the present age groups up to thirty was very close at hand in so far as the calling of men for military training and subsequent service in the army for the duration of the war is concerned. It is fairly easy to determine that that state of affairs exists because there will be no more men forthcoming in that area.
With regard to the other administrative divisions I indicated likewise that there were

War Appropriation-War Services
at least two divisions where we would soon be in that situation. With regard to other divisions I indicated that we would not know the real extent of the man-power reserve that still exists until we had felt the full impact of the agricultural and other regulations.
In each division we know the number of single men there are by age groups. We likewise know the number of men we have called. We know the number of men to whom we have sent notices to report for medical examination. But I could not give the figures at the moment by age groups of the number of men who have enlisted. That would involve a review of attestation papers, because, so far as I am aware, enlistments are not recorded by age groups. That information could be obtained but it would require a great deal of work.
Does the minister say there is no record kept showing by age groups the number of men who have voluntarily enlisted?
The number of men who have enlisted is certainly available.
Yes, and their ages.
I do not know that there is a record kept by the Department of National Defence of enlistments by individual ages. I do not see what advantage there would be in having such a record.
They do not take them under eighteen or over a certain age, so that they must have knowledge of their ages.
They have the ages on the attestation papers.
And that is available to the minister.
I have no doubt that that information could be obtained, but I imagine it would take a good deal of work and time to get it. I doubt very much whether the enlistments are recorded by individual ages.

Then how can the minister know that the numbers in a certain age group are almost exhausted? The minister knows the number of available men in the different age groups through the national registration; how can he say that the numbers in any age group are nearing exhaustion if he does not know the number in that age group who have enlisted?
It is easy to see the situation when there are no more men available.
How?

Because there are no more men to receive notices. It is one thing to know when the state of exhaustion has been arrived at in a particular division, but it is quite another thing to know how many men are still available in another division-quite a different thing. In respect of the divisions where there are still men available the information as to how many are available in those divisions cannot be given without an immense amount of work. Some divisions must reach a state of exhaustion of the man-power reserve before others. The divisions cannot all go forward at exactly the same pace. You may reach the stage of exhaustion in one division before you do in another.
How does the minister arrive at the conclusion that the numbers of men within a certain age group in a certain district have almost reached the point of exhaustion?
Because there are no more cards and no more persons to send notices to.

What are the two divisions that are practically exhausted?
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	And	the
other two which are approaching that position?

The other one that is very close to exhaustion is administrative division F, Quebec. Another one that is very close to exhaustion is administrative division K, Vancouver.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	And	the
other two?

I mentioned only three. I have named administrative division C, and the other two I have in mind are administrative division F, Quebec, and administrative division K, Vancouver.
Mr.	HANSON	(York-Sunbury):	I understood the minister to refer to two other administrative divisions.
Mr.	THORSON: No.

Then I misapprehended. The information asked for this afternoon is of extreme importance. The minister has stated in reply to the hon. member for Carleton that by counting the cards it is easy enough to arrive at the situation in divisions which are near exhaustion. If I appreciate the machinery correctly, there is, to start off with, a given number of cards in a given administrative district, and they are divided into age groups. That is possibly the only visible result of the national registration

War Appropriation-Agriculture
of which the country is aware. The call for volunteers comes and certain numbers in those different age groups volunteer. That information filters through and their cards are eliminated from the records in the minister's department. Certain names are eliminated, and there are so many left. Surely by the process of eliminating those who have gone through the volunteer stage it is simple enough to count the number of cards left and determine the number of men available, by exactly the same process as that by which the minister arrives at the conclusion that in a certain administrative division, C, the reserve is near exhaustion.
We cannot accept the minister's answer. It does not make sense. It is an evasion of responsibility on the part of the administration to withhold this information from us. We shall insist on having it between now and the time of the debate on the mobilization act. It is our right to have the information. It is possible to get it, and we shall insist on having it. None of the difficulties to which the minister has referred is of any great importance.	.

It was stated last night that to-day we might discuss the war appropriation bill under different departments which are indicated in Hansard, and the Minister of Agriculture said that he would be prepared to answer questions. I should like to ask him two or three questions regarding agriculture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I wonder if we cannot by mutual consent organize this discussion to some extent. If agriculture is to be taken up now with the consent of the committee, and if the committee will stick to agriculture until it is through, I do not think there will be any objection.
It is the first item there.
That is a perfectly proper proposal; start on one and finish it.
I was simply starting out in accordance with the procedure suggested by the minister last night at the adjournment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee may make any suggestions as regards the procedure it will follow, but, as suggested by the Minister of Finance, it will make for greater clarity of the record if one department is finished with before.another department is taken up. If that is the pleasure of the committee we will follow that rule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is obvious that we cannot take a vote as to which department we will go on with. It is the responsibility of the government, and the decision is that agriculture be proceeded with now.
That is settled?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The production of poultry and eggs affects more farmers than that of any other agricultural commodity in Canada at the present time. I believe the minister realizes that a great deal has been done to encourage the development and expansion of these products. It has been pointed out to me, by people who I think should know, that in the near future there may be difficulty in selling these products to Great Britain. They claim they have been told that the food ministry of Great Britain can procure these articles through the lease-lend law of the United States much more easily than they can get them from Canada. I think the minister should tell us what provision was made, respecting the billion-dollar gift to Great Britain, for the supply of agricultural products -not merely those I have named, but others as well-in order that the producers may have some idea as to what the marketing possibilities of these products will be.
On page 2921 of Hansard there is an item, under wartime prices and trade board, of administration, S3,380,000, and another item, subsidies under price ceiling order, $50,000,000. The minister might explain the break-down under those two heads.
It may be a little out of order, but I do not think it is premature to ask the minister if he has any thought of making provision under the price ceiling regulations for harvest wages this fall. We had some serious difficulties last fall in the harvesting of our crop. There were people going through the country who were not eager to work and were demanding rates of pay some of which were ridiculous. It has been pointed out here that when this price ceiling was set on agricultural products, many items were fixed at far below the cost of production. If agriculture must produce on that basis, surely the government should take steps to regulate wages in the production of those necessary articles. The people who are going to work on the farms this fall should receive fair remuneration, but the government should step in and set a scale of wages covering the services which these men will give in the harvesting of the crops.

War Appropriation-Agriculture

I do not know whether I can keep in mind all the questions which were raised by the hon. member, but if I miss any of them he can ask them again.
I believe the first suggestion was that I explain to the committee just what is the position in relation to eggs and poultry. It will be recalled by hon. members that at the beginning of the war we set up the agricultural supplies board, which is composed of six of the officials of the department-the four heads of the different divisions, and the assistant deputy as well as the executive assistant. This committee has working under it special boards which deal with different products. We have the bacon board, which deals with pork products; the dairy board, which deals with dairy products, and a special products board, which divides its activities into two sections, the poultry products section and the fruit and vegetables section. They enter into negotiations with the British government with regard to the production and the marketing of the different products in Great Britain.
So far as poultry is concerned arrangements have been made for the marketing of eggs. Since the poultry section was created in April, 1941, the board has entered into contracts with the British Ministry of Food for supplies of Canadian eggs and has handled all shipments of eggs to the United Kingdom. Contracts and shipments of eggs are as follows:
In 1941 the contract was for 460,000 cases, and we supplied 457,451 cases.
In 1942 the contract was for 1,500,000 cases, and there have been supplied, of shelled eggs, 367,608 cases. On February 6, 1942, instructions were received from Britain to forward the remaining quantity, that is the remaining part of the larger order of last year, the 1942 crop, as dried eggs. Shipments in shell to that date totalled 137,630 cases, leaving 1,362,370 cases to be dried. We have three egg-drying plants, one at Toronto, one at Winnipeg, and one at Saskatoon. These were brought into immediate operation to dry eggs for the board. Milk-drying plants at Ottawa, Gananoque, and Belmont, in Ontario, were converted into egg-drying plants, and additional drying plants are being constructed under private auspices at Toronto, Winnipeg, Calgary and Edmonton. The plant at Saskatoon is being enlarged. These plants are being constructed under agreement with the Canadian government. Their period of usefulness is expected to end at the close of the war. Certain assistance therefore has been given in connection with the setting up of those plants.

I think that is all that it is necessary to say with regard to the egg contracts. They have resulted in all the surplus eggs being taken from the Canadian market and sent to Great Britain.
Are the returns from the dried eggs to the farmer as great as they were when the eggs were sold in the shell?
My understanding is that they will be. The prices remain as they were arranged for in the contract.
The minister did not state the selling price of the eggs to the British board. Has he that information available?

The original agreement was for eggs at 28 cents during the high production season and at 32 cents at another period-I have not the exact months before me. Later we arranged to add 3 cents to that price, the amount being taken out of the treasury of Canada, to make it up to 31 and 35 cents.
Would the minister care to make a statement on the beef situation in Toronto under this agriculture item, on the wartime prices and trade board-
Could we have a little sequence to this? The minister has only started to answer the questions I asked.
What was the next item mentioned by the hon. member?
I asked if the minister could give us an idea as to the different types and amounts of agricultural products that have been or will be included under the billion dollar gift to Britain.

The question is whether I can give the committee the different amounts of the farm products which will be supplied to Britain under the billion dollar gift. It would be difficult, because of the nature of the agreements themselves, even to make an estimate of what proportion will be taken care of under the billion dollar gift. For example, under the agreements in connection with bacon we enter into an arrangement with Britain as to what price she is prepared to pay for bacon, and then we proceed to supply bacon at that figure. A financial arrangement has been entered into between the Department of Finance and the treasury in Britain, with regard to the division of the billion dollar amount which is a gift by Canada to Great Britain. I am not in possession of the facts, and I doubt very much if the Minister of Finance would be able to say just what proportion of the amount which will be

War Appropriation-Agriculture
required to take care of the total payments for bacon will be charged up to the British treasury, and what proportion eventually will be charged to the government of Canada. I think a near approach to the position can be found by examining past agreements.
Our agreement of last year provided for payment on the basis of 80 shillings. I think if we leave out for the moment places at which payment was to be made, we can get our proportions a little more clearly. The agreement this year calls for a payment of 100 shillings. If we were to say that Britain is not prepared to pay more this year than she paid last year, then it would be obvious that about 25 per cent of the amount paid last year per hundredweight would be expected to come out of the financial arrangements with Canada for this year. But I am not at all certain that it can be stated in such definite terms. Britain was prepared to pay us and did pay at the end of last season 85 shillings, although she contracted to pay only 80 shillings; and there has been an increase therefore from 85 to 100 as compared with the end of last season. But the government here have agreed to advance a billion dollars to Britain which is to be expended for war materials, including food, and some agreement will be made as to the division of the amount as time goes on.
Would wheat be included in that?

It has not been, up to
date, and I am not sure whether it will.

There was another
question-whether the harvest wages will be taken care of under the price ceiling structure.

I can only say that
the prices board is under the control of the Department of Finance, and the labour situation is under the control of the Labour department. All we do in connection with agriculture is to make representations to them from time to time as to what the labour situation is in agriculture, and make any suggestions we can as to how it might be dealt with. I think this matter would be better discussed when one of the ministers is before the committee.

Then there is the
850,000,000 subsidy under the price ceiling order. How is it divided? What products does it cover, and to whom are the different amounts paid?

That comes not under
my department but under the Department of Finance.
How much is going to agriculture? Does the minister not know?
The amount was stated in Hansard yesterday at page 2920. It is $11,042,281.

On the
same page there is an item under the head of Finance, "Subsidies under the price ceiling order, $50,000,000." What proportion is to go to agriculture?
Where does that appear?

Near the
bottom of the page.

That is under the
Department of Finance. I have no knowledge as to what these subsidies are apart from what we have seen from time to time as applied to certain products. There were subsidies in connection with milk and certain juices and things of that sort. That is entirely under the war prices board and comes under finance.
Then there is an amount of $3,700,000 in connection with disposal of agricultural products.
That has no connection with the other.
Assistance given in disposing of surplus agricultural products.
I wish to urge upon the minister that heed be given to the suggestions which have been thrown out with regard to the harvest months this fall. The farmers are very much interested in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will pass them on to the Minister of Labour.

I suggest that the minister
should take each of these items separately and give an explanation. There are eight or ten items amounting to $11,000,000 and it would be better if, instead of his being asked a separate question under each item, he would make a general statement giving us an idea as to how the money is to be expended under the various items.

I agree
with that; it is an orderly way to proceed. I should like the minister to give a statement with respect to the $3,700,000 for the disposal of agricultural products rendered surplus by the war. There is still, I assume, an apple situation in Nova Scotia. This is a distressed industry owing, to the fact that we cannot find bottoms to ship Nova Scotia apples to the

War Appropriation-Agriculture
other side. It would be interesting to know whether the government is subsidizing farmers in the Annapolis valley to-day in a class of work which good apple husbandry requires them to do themselves. I am told that the farmers in the Annapolis valley are receiving a subsidy to take out the old mature dying and dead trees in their orchards. That is something they should do as a matter of course, but with respect to assistance in the disposal of surplus crop, this government has assumed an obligation and should continue to carry it until some other disposition of the crop is made. How far are we carrying this agricultural assistance? Members from the east would like to know.
There is a further question on the million dollars for fertilizers. I should like to know what is being done in that regard. I am told that not one dollar of it is going to the potato farmers; it is going among other farmers. Why the discrimination against potato farmers in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island? These are pertinent questions on which we should have some information.
I do not think there are any potato farmers getting a subsidy.
I understand that is so; but why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is an explanation. Mr. HANSON (York-Sunbury): There may be, but let us have the reason for it. There may be a good reason, but the farmers do not understand it. They think it is rank discrimination against them. I do not say it is, and I am prepared to wait until we hear the explanation before passing judgment.
I should like to ask the minister a question with reference to potato production in this country. According to a Canadian Press dispatch dated Ottawa June 1, entitled "Canada raises potato output for U.S.A.," it is announced that:
Joint Canadian-United States action to increase the Canadian potato production for sale in the United States and to step up Canadian output of hog products was announced to-day by the agriculture department.
The plans, which have received formal approval of the Canadian government, follow recommendations of the joint economic committee of Canada and the United States.
I am more particularly interested in the potato part, which follows:
The potato arrangement provides that steps will be taken to increase Canadian potato production, for sale as table stock in the United States in the event of a short crop in that country or for manufacture into starch for lease-lend shipment if United States production meets table needs.
The United States has undertaken to purchase up to five million bushels of Canadian EMr, It. B. Hanson.]
potatoes for conversion to starch. These will be purchased at the prevailing United States prices for starch potatoes in the area of processing.
That of course will be a low price.
Under the announced price programme the floor price for United States No. 1 potatoes at Aroostook, Me., is $1.25 a hundredweight sacked and loaded f.o.b. cars.
Present indications are that production in Canada and the United States will be below the domestic requirements of north America for seed and current needs, including starch.
Existing trade agreements provide that if the United States' production goes below 350,000,000 bushels, the Canadian quota admissible to the United States at a reduced rate of duty is increased automatically by the amount which the United States crop is below the 350,000,000.
Agriculture officials at Washington report it is likely that under this agreement between
9.000.000 and 10,000,000 bushels may be added to the Canadian quota this year.
That is very substantial. But this is the second day of June; this announcement is just out. Have our potato growers in Canada been apprised in advance in order that they may make preparation for this increase in production? I understand that the acreage in potatoes in New Brunswick has been substantially reduced and that no preparations are being made to meet this immense increase in our quota to the United States. I welcome it, make no mistake about that; for a long time we have wanted to get that market. We have always met resistance from the Aroostook farmers. They have been strong enough with their great fruit and vegetable growers' organization to keep our product out, whereas, per contra, their influence with their government has been strong enough to prevent Canada from imposing an exchange duty against their products. Hence we have no exchange duty against early vegetables coming to this country, and have been limited to a more or less miserable quota for good table potato stock going to the United States.
I welcome this reported arrangement. It is a fine demonstration of how people can come together during war time. Besides asking whether this report is true, as I assume it is, I should like to know whether the potato farmers of Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have been notified in time to enable them to take advantage of what looks like a good opportunity for increased production. Have the agricultural supply boards been informing the farmers? I am afraid it is too late if the word has not already gone out. I read the local papers from my province every day and I -have not seen in them a word about this. It is

War Appropriation-Agriculture
now the second day of June, and if the farmers have not the seed and fertilizer and the ground ready, it is a month too late.
And this year's crop is all sold.

The trade agreement between Canada and the United States, which has been discussed in this house, sets up the conditions under which we trade with them ir potatoes among other things. The recommendations of the international economic committee which was set up to consider matters of this kind were made about a month ago. That -was first considered here; then it had to go to Washington and be considered there, and there was no possibility of making an announcement earlier than yesterday. It will be realized that there is no possibility of either the United States government or the Canadian government determining at this time whether more potatoes will be required in the United States, for the very reason indicated a moment ago. We have just passed or are just at the seeding season for potatoes in many parts of the continent.
The acreage is one indication.

Yes, and the weather is another. For the last two or three years, probably in any year, our potato acreage has been sufficient to supply our own market plus any other markets we could find. Our difficulty has been a surplus; it is not a matter of acreage. The United States people came to us with the suggestion that this year there is a possibility of an acreage shortage, or that even if they have as high an acreage as usual this was probably not going to be a particularly good potato year in certain parts of the United States, and they asked if this country would make whatever provision we could, without running ourselves into serious difficulties, to provide for the situation. We made a careful survey of the situation in Canada and we think the acreage being put into potatoes will take care of any possible demands, provided we have an average or better than average crop.
Will the minister indicate what that survey reveals? Is there a reduction in acreage? My understanding is that there is a definite reduction in New Brunswick.

Possibly there is in New Brunswick. I am not certain whether there is a reduction across Canada. I do not think anyone can say definitely, because in certain parts of Canada we are just about at planting time; around May 24 is planting time for
potatoes. At any rate it was thought the acreage was going to be at a level which would produce the potatoes that might be required in the United States. I think the leader of the opposition will agree that it would put the Canadian farmer in as serious a position to have a production larger than the market could take care of, as it would to have the acreage a little below the average.
Well, he is used to that.

You might run into more difficulty with the one result than the other. The opinion of officials, for what it is worth- and they are dealing with the problem all the time-is that we shall have sufficient acreage, if we have an average crop or better, to take care of the possible requirements indicated by the United States. They have not yet said they will require them, and it would not be good policy to start boosting acreage in Canada on the assumption that there may be a poor crop in the United States. But we welcome the suggestion of the United States authorities that if that does happen they will look first to Canada for their additional supplies.

They have no other place to look. I am not raising this question in any querulous spirit. I am just suggesting that if they are looking for increased production in Canada we are too late, having taken a month to consider the position. The information I have is that the acreage is being reduced. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield) who is probably one of the biggest growers of potatoes in New Brunswick, has reduced his acreage this year by nearly 50 per cent. I understand from him that that is symptomatic of the whole position. If that be so, we will have just about enough potatoes for our own market, which of course is the position I have advocated for years. Until we have a better entry into the United States market we had better not have a surplus. The minister is on solid ground in suggesting that. But if it is probable that the United States will take more of our production, then the point I am endeavouring to make is that we are late in notifying the Canadian grower.
Would the minister mind saying a word with respect to fertilizers? There is some disappointment and misunderstanding in the country on that point.
I wonder if the leader of the opposition would allow me to proceed in the manner he suggested at the beginning of his remarks.

All right.
War Appropriation-Agriculture
He suggested that I follow right through the different items; then if there are any questions to ask we can have them.
I have finished, so far as I am concerned.

If that is the desire of the committee I shall deal with the different items. The first is one of $34,502 for administration, made up of salaries, $18,000; cost of living bonus, $502; printing and stationery, $4,000; telephone and telegraph, $1,000; travelling expenses, $9,000, and miscellaneous, $2,000.
The first item following administration stands in the name of the flax fibre administrator.
With respect to the salaries under the administration item, are those additional salaries?
Yes, those are additional.
Salaries paid to personnel engaged by the board?
Yes, those are in addition to the salaries paid to the regular staff. The members of the board itself are not paid any salary over and above what they get from the department.

What is the beef situation to-day? Is there any chance of relief? I ask the question because in Peterborough and adjacent towns last Saturday there was no beef or lamb to be had. Not only the storekeepers but the people generally are affected.

I again appeal to the committee to permit me to follow the suggestion made a few minutes ago, that I take this up item by item. I believe if that is done we can go through the list in a short time.
It will be recalled that at the beginning of the war we were asked to provide additional fibre flax in Canada. In order to avoid a difficulty experienced during the last war, when the seed went up to a very high price, we took possession of the seed and set up a fibre flax administrator under the war supplies board. That official makes provision for its distribution to increase our acreage in Canada. The remainder of it is supplied to Great Britain, to increase fibre flax supplies in the old country.
Do these administrators come under the agricultural supplies board?
Yes.

Who is the administrator?
[Mr. R. B. Hanson.3
The head of it is Dean Shaw. Administration costs in connection with fibre flax are placed at $22,780.
Does this deal with the disposal of the flax?

It deals largely with the disposal of the seed, and it makes arrangements under which the fibre flax itself will go to the proper places. Under this item salaries stand at $11,980; senior flax inspector, $2,400; five regional flax inspectors, $7,500; one stenographer, $1,080; cost of living bonus $1,000; printing and stationery, $500; telephone and telegraph $300; travelling expenses, $9,500, and miscellaneous, $500.
The next item is for fertilizer and pesticides.
What steps are being taken to utilize the straw of the flax being grown in the west? I understand it is too short to be used as fibre, but has great value as tow.

I am not just certain as to the value of the flax grown in the west, so far as its use for fibre is concerned. Hon. members from Saskatchewan and probably from some other parts of Canada will remember that for a long time in Saskatchewan we experimented with flax straw. A gentleman who was proficient in making a kind of twine and other materials from flax straw was engaged by the Saskatchewan government. The difficulty was that we were never able to produce it at commercial values; therefore we did not accomplish very much by way of giving assistance in the production of flax products. I do not know that the condition is different even yet. Flax in western Canada is grown in a dry climate, with the result that the fibre breaks into short lengths when handled. Those short lengths are not nearly as valuable for the making of linens or twines as are the long fibres of the fibre flax.
Does that apply to the irrigated areas?
Yes; I think the climate is the important factor, rather than that the water is made available at the roots. At least that is my information, so far as my experience goes.

Flax grown in the west is not used at all in the manufacture of linens, because it is not suitable for that purpose. An entirely different seed is sown in Ontario and Quebec, where flax fibres are produced. There is no flax fibre in the west, and never was.

It is being grown in the Fraser' valley to make linens.

I am speaking of the
prairie provinces.
It is grown in Manitoba, at Portage la Prairie.

I suggest to the minister that if he goes right through and then we begin to ask questions, it will take a long time. If at the end of each item he would pause and answer the questions, . and then proceed to the next item, he would not have to come back. It could be done more expeditiously in this way than by having a general debate all over again.

War Appropriation-Agriculture
Canada and in British Columbia in order that we might have a greater production of meats and fats and dairy products.
It was not thought wise to provide assistance in connection with commodities of which we have a surplus already. For example, since the war started we have been paying out money year after year to take care of our apple crop. A year ago we had trouble in carying our potato crop, but we did not have so much difficulty this past year because there was a poor crop. However, we are not expecting to have poor crops every year. In other words, it has not been necessary to increase our production of potatoes or our production of apples or our production of most vegetables in order to get the supplies that are required in connection with our war effort. So that no assistance is being given in that direction; the assistance is being given to get coarse grains, and the fertilizers provided for must be applied to lands on which coarse grains are being grown.
Since the beginning of the war we have had a seeds administration, which costs $9,498,
made up as follows:
Salaries	 $4,598
Printing and stationery	 COO
Telephones and telegraphs	 600
Travelling expenses	 3,000
Miscellaneous	 700
An order in council passed on January 16, 1942, authorized the appointment of a seeds administrator to regulate the distribution of field crop and garden vegetable seeds to meet present and potential needs. It will be recalled that before the war we were getting many of our garden seeds from European countries. Immediately the war started there was a blockade and it was impossible for us to obtain seeds from that source. This organization was set up to encourage the production of garden seeds in Canada, and we have experienced no difficulty in getting sufficient garden seeds to be able to carry on down to the present time.
Then we have a flour and feeds administration, at a cost of $55,000, made up as follows:
Salaries	 $25,000
Printing and stationery	 14,000
Travelling expenses	 6,000
Miscellaneous, including telephones
and telegraphs	 10,000
The greater part of the activities of the feeds administrator has to do with the shipment of feed grain from the prairie west into the eastern part of Canada, and from the prairie west into British Columbia. I think hon. members are fairly familiar with the provisions of the agreement. In 1940 provision was made for the payment of a proportionate cost to those provinces which 
undertook to apply the policy and pay the remaining part of the cost. Ontario was the only province that undertook that policy. In 1942 we agreed to pay the entire freight from Fort William east and from Calgary and Edmonton west on feed grain shipped from the prairie provinces into, other sections of Canada. Under that system all provinces have been importing feed grain from western Canada down to the present time. We have under consideration at the moment-and I say this because it is something which is of interest to farmers, particularly in eastern Canada and British Columbia-the question whether this arrangement will be renewed on the present basis. The present agreement terminates on June 30, and it will be necessary to inform business men in different parts of Canada whether or not it is expected to terminate it at the end of June. I hope to have a final decision on the question within a week, and to be able to announce what position we will be taking for the coming year with regard to the shipment of feed grains.
The next item is programmes to encourage the production of essential war supplies. It is estimated that these programmes will cost $230,000 this year. The first item is advertising, and the first item under advertising is the crop production programme for the prairie provinces for 1942. The purpose of that programme is to acquaint the prairie farmer with the government's crop production programme for 1942, which was framed according to the requirements of war conditions. This has been announced already and it was discussed quite thoroughly in the early part of the session. This advertising was put out in March and April, 1942, and the media used were the daily and weekly newspapers and the farm press circulating in western Canada, as well as posters and leaflets outlining the crop programme. The cost of that was S15,000.
Item number two is the bacon and hog programme. The purpose of this is to encourage and assist in the production of quality hogs in sufficient quantity to supply the hog products required by Britain. There was one advertisement each month, and the media were the farm papers of Canada and certain foreign news weeklies. The cost is approximately $6,000 per month. We were successful in each of the preceding years in obtaining for Britain all the bacon and ham we contracted to supply. During this present year we have contracted to supply Britain with 600 million pounds. The last reports I have indicate that we have secured-and I say secured, because it is not possible to keep shipments up with deliveries in view of conditions prevailing on the

War Appropriation-Agriculture
Atlantic-we have secured for shipment to Britain in the first twenty-five weeks of the present year 52 per cent of the total required to supply that 600 million pounds. The year began with the first of October last. It has just been suggested to me by my colleague that the agreement is not limited to 600 million pounds, but is not less than 600 million pounds, and we are well on the way towards the delivery of that amount during this coming year. We are hopeful that we shall be able to deliver the amount required to fill the minimum of that contract.
Then there is the farm women's campaign. We noticed that during the first year of the war and well on into the second year we had been paying much attention to activities on the part of the men who are providing labour for farms, but not so much to acknowledge and urge greater accomplishments by women who are providing labour on the farm. Every member of the house is aware of the fact that much of the work on every farm, particularly where it is a mixed-dairy or fruit-farming operation, is carried on by women. That always has been and probably always will be so, because of their activities not only in the home itself but outside the home in carrying on some kind of dairy operations, and often poultry and other operations. We have adopted a plan to encourage and assist farm women in carrying out their task in the war, particularly in the production of food. Advertisements commenced in the late May papers, and in the June issues. Six advertisements in the series are to be released at the rate of one a month. Selected farm publications having editors of women's sections are being used. The cost of this series is estimated at $30,000 for the present year.
In December, 1941, the agricultural supplies board secured authority under order in council to place in five Canadian plants already engaged in dehydration work-one in British Columbia, two in Ontario and two in Nova Scotia-the extra equipment required in experimental processing to the new specifications, and to have those plants purchase and process for government account, under supervision of the board's representative, certain quantities of vegetables of 1941 production. Our reason for doing that was this. The British government sent an agent to Canada and to the United States in the year 1940 to inquire into the possibilities of receiving more food products in dehydrated form, the reason being obvious -that you can ship much more in a given space of dehydrated fruits and vegetables than of fruits and vegetables in their natural state. If I remember correctly, dehydrated eggs, for example, take about one-seventh the space
required for shell eggs. The advantages of the dehydrated plan will be obvious in view of the shortage of shipping space caused by war conditions.
When the British agent was here first we had not developed processes which were satisfactory. The British agent went back to Britain and obtained from the records the processes that were being followed in Britain. He brought them back to this country and discussed the matter fully with the officials of the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Trade and Commerce. We developed in cooperation with them a process for dehydrating vegetables and fruits which was satisfactory to Britain, and that process is being applied now in plants across Canada. We have given assistance to the plants in putting in the kind of equipment required fpr this new process, and they are now operating under the plan which was evolved.

But you have not any
orders?

We are sending over
the commodity regularly. Under this project approximately 170 tons of beets were processed, sixty-nine tons of turnips, thirty-one tons of carrots and thirteen tons of cabbage. Considerable quantities of these dried products were placed with the Canadian defence forces for use as emergency rations, particularly in connection with coastal defence work, and as the fiscal year ended attempts were being made to interest British officials in the products. As the member for Yale suggested, British orders are not available up to the moment, but there are not sufficient products available to make shipments in shipload lots possible in view of what we are using in Canada. It is estimated that approximately $225,000 will be expended to complete this work in 1941-42, most of which should be recovered by the sale of the products made. Of the $225,000 estimated to be expended, approximately $22,000 was used to purchase for the plants special equipment, which is owned by the government.
What is the arrangement in that regard? Do the plants pay for it? Does the government take it over after the war?

The arrangement is
contained in an agreement I have here, the terms of which I can read if desired. The proposal is to write off the amount at 20 per cent per year, which would mean a five-year arrangement. It is thought that some of this additional equipment will be useful later on.
The programme for 1942-43 is outlined in the order in council of May 18, 1942, for an



War Appropriation-Agriculture
expenditure of $500,000. It is expected that the programme will follow the same course as in 1941-42, the output being increased by reason of the increased plant equipment.
The purchase, storage and distribution of agricultural supplies is the next item-$1,405,583. Special measures were taken to insure supplies of certain field root and garden vegetable seeds. I explained, when I was dealing with the appointment of the administrator, the plan under which that was done. Provincial seed production committees were formed in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Manitoba, and British Columbia, and the dominion and provincial governments concerned agreed to accept all seed grown on the acreage under contract of a quality equal to registered or certified seed grain. Under this arrangement more than 470 acres of various root and vegetable crops were contracted for, for seed purposes, in 1940. These measures were continued in 1941, and we propose to continue them further in 1942. Under these measures we have produced bean seed, also seed for potato^ cabbage, cauliflower, cucumber, lettuce, onion, tomato, mangel and other vegetables.
Among the other potential amounts required is the sum of $1,000,000 under the heading of purchase, storage and distribution of agricultural supplies, to provide for unseen contingencies in the field of agricultural supplies. An example of what might be needed was the necessity during 1939, 1940 and 1941 of purchasing and distributing fibre flax seed surplus to growers' immediate needs.
That, I think, takes us down to assistance in the disposal of agricultural products rendered surplus by the war-the item specially mentioned, I believe, by the hon. member for Weybum as well as by the leader of the opposition.
The first item mentioned by the leader of the opposition was assistance in apple marketing. In explanation of what has happened in the maritime provinces, in British Columbia, and to some extent in Ontario, I should say that the 1941 apple crop was smaller than that of 1940. It will be recalled that I stated here last session that in the first year of the war the British government were not desirous of taking any apples from Canada. Up to that time they had been taking 50 per cent of our crop. That required 80 per cent of the maritime province crop, about 50 per cent of the crop from British Columbia, but very little of the crop of Ontario, with the result that about 50 per cent of the apple crop was going to the British market. When war was declared Britain said that she did not wish to have any apples, because they took up too much shipping space and had little

food value compared with other foodstuffs. Finally however they agreed to take half the quantity of the preceding year. They did not desire to take any of the 1940 crop. Fortunately we did not have in that year as large a crop, and our difficulties in disposing of it were not quite as great. In 1941 again we entered into an arrangement under which the British government took part of the crop from Canada, and we had to take care of the remainder of it in this country. The 1941 apple crop was smaller than that of 1940, but since, early in the season, there was no indication that Britain would take fresh apples, arrangements were made to assist in the marketing of the Nova Scotia and British Columbia crop. In September, 1941, the British Ministry of Food decided to take 1,200,000 boxes and 110,000 barrels of Canadian apples in the fresh state. Owing to the export of these apples from British Columbia, Nova Scotia and to a lesser extent from Ontario, Ontario apple growers did not require any dominion assistance. They sold their apples at, as has been said, good prices in the central part of Canada. We had agreements with British Columbia. I do not know that the committee will want me to go into the details of those agreements. In 1941 we had no agreement with Ontario, but we did have an agreement with Nova Scotia. The agreement with New Brunswick involved 4,600,000 boxes; in Nova Scotia it involved 1,500,000 barrels. The total expenditures during the year ended March 31, 1942, were as follows: In relation to British Columbia apples, further expenditures under the 1940-41 agreement were $181,810.04; under the 1941-42 agreement, $311,230.68. In Ontario the expenditure for 1940-41 was very small, only $3,819.10. In Nova Scotia, further expenditures under the
1940-	41 agreement which had to be made in the succeeding year were $124,96124; under the
1941-	42 agreement, $1,649,160.92. Further expenditures under this latter agreement will have to be made.
An agreement has already been concluded with Nova Scotia somewhat along the lines of the previous agreements for the crop of 1942. We shall have negotiations with Ontario with regard to their position. An agreement is under discussion with British Columbia but has not yet been made.
Were these net figures of expenditures on apples?

Yes. These are the net figures which have been paid out under the similar vote in the preceding years, and this vote which is set up now will be applied to similar purposes.

After the evaporated fruit and other products have been disposed of?
Yes. I think that is correct, but I will make sure.

I do not know
whether I am in order. Am I to understand that I must follow through the board administration, and so on down the line, and ask the minister any questions in that order?

I do not think it. is
necessary to follow through item by item. That completes everything down to assistance in the disposal of agricultural products rendered surplus by the war. I think it would be just as well if we stopped there and had any questions which hon. members may wish to ask. The items below that are: bacon board, dairy produots board, special products board, freight assistance on western feed grain, and fertilizer assistance. These are special items which I think we can discuss by themselves, and it might be better to deal with each of them separately rather than fry to give an outline of them all.

That is the reason I am asking the question. Naturally, coming from a British Columbia rural district, I am more particularly interested in the dairy products board, but I do not know whether I am in order in asking any questions at this time. There have been so many rulings.

I suggest that we take the last five items one by one, and if there are any questions on what I have been discussing, they can be asked now. We will take the bacon board next, and then the dairy board, and have questions on each one.

Under this item of assistance in the disposal of agricultural products, the minister mentioned only one article, and that was apples. It does not seem possible that all this money would be taken up with the disposal of the surplus apple crop. Are there not some other items for which assistance is needed as well?

That is the product
which has had practically all the assistance that has been given in the way of amounts paid out of this sum this year. The amount which will be required for dealing with the situation during this coming year will not, of course, total the full amount of this sum, which is S3,700,000. In round figures the amount which we have used in connection with apples during the last number of years has been about $2,000,000. The figures which I have given, it will be noted, are not complete. The sums paid out during the last financial
year partly had to do with the preceding financial year, and partly related to the last financial year, but the figures are not complete as at the end of the last financial year. Speaking from memory, the total amount spent on apples has been a little over $2,000,000.
With regard to this assistance which has been given, I think, the way it is put, it surely means that the government early realized that that was a war casualty.
Yes.

That was the reason. The export was suddenly cut off; the producers of apples in the three provinces mentioned were without a very considerable slice of their market; it had to be replaced, and the dominion government recognized that fact. I have a question to ask with regard to the preceding item, having to do with assistance in dehydration to try to meet the British demand. I think I am right in saying that in the last war Great Britain had a pretty disappointing experience with the quality of the dehydrated products.
In order to overcome that difficulty the government established certain experimental works in five factories for the purpose of endeavouring to reach the high standard of dehydration which Great Britain demanded. Some of these experiments were carried on in my neighbourhood and I know how successful the result has been as far as it has gone; and the assistance given by the department has been I think very greatly appreciated by the industry. But the difficulty comes in with regard to what happens next. Two months ago the manager of that industry was in touch with me in an endeavour to find out what prospect there would be of marketing if he went ahead and grew vegetables himself and advised those who usually deal with him to grow vegetables, for the purpose of marketing the stuff under the agreement with Great Britain. I was not able to obtain any information with regard to the prospect of that marketing. Can the minister say anything about the difficulty which lies ahead? Obviously dehydration plants will not proceed to induce farmers to grow if they do not see ahead to the marketing of the product. For war purposes these dehydration products are wanted for the supply of Britain for the forces, and for our Canadian forces as well, and world markets are not open to them.
The objective of the department so far has been merely to conduct this as an experimental undertaking.

To demonstrate that it can be done.

War Appropriation-Agriculture

To demonstrate the usefulness of the process by which dehydration is to be carried out. The hon. member is correct in stating that the experiences of the last war are still in the minds of the British government and of the Canadian government. An effort is being made to evolve a process that will satisfactorily dehydrate fruit and vegetables and place them over in Britain in proper shape. I think both the British government and the dominion government are well satisfied with the experiments that have been carried on this year, and as the hon. member has stated, those in his area are well satisfied. We think it will be a success. The amount of money provided this year is about double what was provided last year, but we do not intend to increase the output beyond what we have the means of disposing of at the moment. We can of course dispose of as much, with the Canadian forces, as we did last year and probably considerably more, but on the other hand if it is required in Great Britain, if the whole quantity is needed there, we can ship it and use fresh vegetables on this side. So that whatever happens in connection with it, I do not think there is much possibility of anyone taking a loss from the experiment. The experiment is worth carrying out in war time because of its usefulness at all times.

In accordance with the order in council of May 18, $50,000 was set aside for equipment assistance in dehydration plants. Will that be used to place equipment in new plants? Potatoes are the chief commodity, 75 per cent being dehydrated, and there are no plants in the surplus producing counties at the present time. I should like to know whether any of this money will be used to assist new plants in the potato producing provinces such as Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.

The intention is of course to make the fullest possible use of the plants that have already been provided with special equipment, and it is hoped that we may be able to extend the activities this year to take in some other areas not covered by the plants last year. But I should not like to go on record with regard to the places at which they will be established, though I am quite sure they will be established to meet areas that have not already been provided with plants, at any time that new plants are put in.
It is not feasible to dehydrate potatoes in plants which are not located in potato producing centres, because you are only shipping 90 per cent water to the plants.
Where are Prince Edward Island potatoes to be dehydrated?
The only plant that is being operated at the moment to which they would likely be shipped is in Nova Scotia, but that is because there was a plant there to which equipment has been added.

I should like to know something in regard to the evaporating of eggs. Have we any hope of getting an export freight rate for crates going to the evaporating plants? We get an export freight rate from the plant to seaboard, but we pay domestic freight rates from our towns to the evaporating plants. On the American side they have an export freight rate from the towns to the evaporating plants-in some of the states, not all. I thought perhaps we might be able to secure that in Canada. We have our plants a considerable distance from egg centres and it costs 52 cents to ship the crate, 11 cents to return the crate, and a charge of 3 cents for the revamping of the crate. What price is given to the evaporated eggs when they are dried? I should like to know what assistance is given to the evaporating plants, such as Swifts of Toronto.
I have not the agreement with me. It has been finally drafted within the last few days and I am not in a position at the moment to give the details of it.
Perhaps at another time.

The only agreement which so far has been finally drawn is the agreement with the plant that is being enlarged at Winnipeg, and that is to be made the basis of other agreements that are entered into with other plants across Canada. I regret however that I have not the details with me. With regard to freight rates, there is quite a difference betvreen freight arrangements in the United States and those in Canada. As every hon. member knows, our rates are pretty much under the control of the transport board and have to be referred to them from time to time as changes are requested. I cannot give any information in that regard.

I should like to ask the minister a question regarding the freight assistance to the western and eastern provinces. The minister pointed out that he was considering, or some board was, the advisability of continuing that policy. If the freight assistance is discontinued it will greatly affect farmers in the Fraser valley. There is no doubt that the assistance given on mill feeds and

War Appropriation-Agriculture
grains has enabled them to carry on, and I strongly urge upon the minister that he continue that policy.
I am not sure whether the price of butter and cheese comes under the minister's department-perhaps it is under the Minister of Finance; that is one of those confusing things. But the price of thirty-five cents set for butter and fifty cents for cheese has reacted on the price of milk and is driving the farmers of the Fraser valley out of business. I am not going to deal with that now because it will come later-
There is no set price of fifty cents on cheese.

For butter it has been set at thirty-five cents, and fifty cents is the equivalent for cheese. That has brought about a situation in Canada under which, according to the figures I have, this year we are already short something like 5,000,000 pounds of butter. In 1941 the consumption was 369,413,809 pounds. From January to April this year we produced 48,803,071 pounds. At the end of April we are 4,485,990 pounds short as compared with 1941. The minister of agriculture for British Columbia, speaking at a meeting a short time ago, said it was unfair that the dairymen should be required to carry such a load of sacrifice as they were carrying at present under shrinking incomes and rising costs. That I think bears out what I was saying a moment ago, that if freight assistance is not continued and no subsidy is given to the farmers, and the price of butter is kept at thirty-five cents, it will mean that the farmers will very largely go out of business, except those who are fairly well established or have considerable bank accounts.
I want to ask the minister what assistance has been given regarding flax. He mentioned five regional officers. I should like to know if one has been appointed for British Columbia, and what assistance is being given. British Columbia this year has contributed S3,000 to a cooperative organization of farmers who are endeavouring to produce a crop of flax. I am not giving it as my opinion, but it is the opinion of experts that they can grow excellent flax for linen in the Fraser valley.
I noticed the other day that Great Britain is sending one of her outstanding agricultural experts to this country, to be attached to the office of the high commissioner. It was stated that his duties in Canada would be to promote the growing of food crops required by the people of Great Britain. It is unlikely that there would be a fibre flax man in the prairie provinces, because we do not grow fibre flax there. I presume they will be chiefly in eastern Canada and British Columbia.
As to the British representative, I may say that Doctor A. Scott Watson-I presume it is he who is referred to-arrived in Halifax from Britain two or three days ago. He did not go first to Washington but came direct to Ottawa and spent part of the day before yesterday and yesterday here. He may be in Ottawa still. When he arrived he naturally came to the Department of Agriculture. I take it his mission in Canada and the United States is to make known in these countries what Britain finds it possible to produce and how much of the different products that she requires during the war period we in Canada and the United States will be able to supply. I do not think there will be any difficulty in coordinating the work of the British representative with the departments of agriculture in Canada and the United States. It is simply a matter of getting first-hand knowledge of British conditions, placing that information before us and finding out what we can do in order to make up the shortage in Britain of those different products. He will of course acquaint his government with the facts, and if the total is not made up they may adjust

War Appropriation-Agriculture
their agriculture in Britain to try to produce more of certain things and less of others in order to fit in with our situation. I think that is the real object of his visit.
With regard to butter I think all who are familiar with dairy production in Canada agree that if we desire to increase production over that of last year the present price will not bring about that increase. There is some doubt in the minds of some whether the present price will produce even the quantity we had last year. The difference of opinion is based on certain facts. We have been in the habit in Canada of thinking that the greater part of the butter we produce, I think about five-sixths, must be produced in the summer months. During all the years we have been producing butter, we have been producing a very considerable part of it in the summer months, and we have had the idea that we can produce butter to good advantage only in the summer months. The result has been that a very considerable storage from the months of May and June is carried over into the winter months in order to keep up our supplies in those winter months.
Last year we had an experience which some people argue disproves our experience of the past. Last summer we had a price for cheese of 16 cents a pound, plus the premium paid by the federal government and subsidies paid by the provincial governments. That brought the price up to between 19 and 20 cents a pound. Under that plan we secured enough cheese to supply the British contract during the summer months, but we had nothing left for the home market. I think members of the committee who are familiar with the facts will agree that it was always thought to be more difficult in the winter months to produce cheese than to produce butter. Last summer cheese was selling on the market at, I believe, about 37 cents a pound. When the wartime prices and trade board established their ceiling prices last fall, that price was not acknowledged as the ceiling price, although cheese sold as high as about 37 c.ents a pound. The reason given for its not being acknowledged was that that was cured cheese, carried over from a preceding year, and sold at a very high price because of the shortage on this market brought about by the taking of all the cheese off the Canadian market last summer.
The point I wish to emphasize is that, with the facts before us last fall, after discussions between the prices board and the Department of Agriculture it was arranged to set a

ceiling price on cheese of 25 cents a pound for the winter months, and our cheese production in Canada increased by leaps and bounds during the winter months. I have not the exact figures before me, but I shall have them later, when we are discussing the . regular estimates. I should have had them this afternoon. However, there has been a remarkable increase in cheese production during the winter months. It goes without saying that the cheese will probably be not quite as good as the cheese produced in the summer months, off the grass. Nevertheless it is a very acceptable food product.
With that experience behind us some people are inclined to argue that we can have a ceiling price on butter of 35 cents during the summer months. I should like to say at this point that that is not a declining price. It is scarcely correct to say that we have had a declining return from farm products, and an increased cost; because, after all, the floor price for butter last year was 29i cents in May, 30 cents in June, and I believe in October it was 32 cents. While the price did not drop down to the floor, it was not quite as high as it has been during the early summer months of this year. The price has been hovering round 34 or 35 cents in May of this year, and I presume it will continue at about that level throughout the month of June. The argument of some is that we should start our increase in prices this year along about the month of September or October, and continuing on through the winter. It is suggested that instead of carrying so much butter in storage from the summer months until the winter, we might go into production of butter during the winter months, which would take care of our needs next winter. There are some agricultural experts who do not agree that we will get that result to the extent we hope to get it. But I am repeating to the committee the strongest argument I have heard from those who take the opposite position. The price as set at the moment is set by the wartime prices and trade board, and the Department of Agriculture is cooperating as far as possible to keep production as high as we can during the summer months. We are hopeful that if no change is made we can go on during the winter months and get greater production in the winter time. That again is an experiment with respect to which no one can exactly foretell the results.
If the argument put forth by the representatives of the prices board does not materialize, then we shall know that we have been wrong in taking that particular position this year in connection with butter, and probably will have to evolve some different plan for a
