succeeding year. We may find as we go along that some other action has to be taken even this year in order to make sure of our supplies -some action which will give further returns. At the moment, however, those who are arguing for the policy being followed take the position that they do not believe that will be necessary, and that we can take care of the situation.

Before the minister leaves this subject may I say, with respect to the apple industry, that I am sure the growers appreciate what the government has done for them in the past two or three years. I understood the minister to say that there was only one dehydration plant in Canada, and that it was situated in Nova Scotia.
No, I thought I said we had five; but I believe the only one available to Prince Edward Island is in Nova Scotia.

In the counties of Northumberland and Durham, I believe there are as many good apples grown as in any other part of Ontario. We are anxious to have a plant established in that district; and if it would be possible for the minister to consider that matter, it would be greatly appreciated. I do not believe there is one within a reasonable distance in that part of the province.

Mr. Chairman, listening to the minister say that what has been done may be wrong, and that we are more or less trying an experiment, it occurs to me that the agricultural war policy of the government has been pretty much one of experiment, trial and error since the war began. That has been the condition from the time we endeavoured to fix the price on bacon. There have been the fixing of winter prices in summer time, the fixing of summer prices in winter time, and a terrific effort to keep prices down.
I recognize the merit in the general principle the government is endeavouring to follow in connection with the price-ceiling policy, but it appears to me that it is almost impossible to carry it out properly. I believe it will prove to be merely an experiment to fix prices on agricultural products, without fixing farmers' costs. The farmer to-day is paying 50 per cent; yes, in many districts he is paying 100 per cent more wages than he paid prior to the war. I suggest there is within sound of my voice no hon. member representing an agricultural constituency who does not know that that is the condition. There have also been great increases in feed costs.
It is true that the government is experimenting with a price-ceiling policy to avoid
inflation in general industry. But those who are associated with industry know very well that wages were fixed. I say in all fairness to the labouring man that some effort should be made to keep his living costs at as low a point as possible. It will be remembered, however, that there is a cost of living bonus, and that wages were frozen and a cost of living bonus added in proportion to the change in the quarterly index. No such situation prevails with respect to agriculture. No wonder it has been said so often that the farmer is the forgotten man of this country. I do not blame the Minister of Agriculture alone for the somewhat economic tanglefoot in which he finds himself, because no doubt he is simply trying to coordinate his policies and efforts with the government's general policy to which I am taking exception at this point.
If we are going to increase agricultural production all along the line, the production of those products that require the most man hours of toil, such as foodstuffs, animal fats, butter, dairy products, meats and so forth, the products which cannot be handled by mass production methods, with the use of heavy machinery, but products which require constant attention in the winter months as well as in the summer months, we must leave some of the old element of chance for a reasonable period to the farmer. He has been living by chance almost since confederation as far as his prices are concerned. Hon. members know that a farmer must be something of a gambler. He must risk weather conditions, whether it will be too wet as it has been the last few days or whether it will be too dry, whether the prices he receives for the products he hopes to produce will pay for the seed, whether he will get less for the one or two offsprings of an animal than he has paid for the breeding animal. He has been forced to take these chances. For ten years the farmers, especially those who produce mixed farm products, have borne the brunt of our economic depression. In depression they were not protected by a floor, in prosperity they are hindered by a ceiling.
These men have not received much in the way of subsidy. For ten years they received only about fifty per cent of what they received in the more normal past for their products. They found it almost impossible to carry on. When war broke out they were appealed to by all of us to produce more. At one time the Minister of Agriculture told them that we did not need more bacon, that the price would be fixed at S9 per 100 pounds in order to keep the price down. When the war started, wages paid to the labouring men in industry were
War Appropriation-Agriculture

fixed, or frozen if you like, but in addition they are paid a cost of living bonus. One result of these higher wages has been that the boy who was working on the farm went to the factory. To-day the farmer must pay practically double the wages he paid in 1939, and there is no cost of living bonus.
Farmers are finding it almost impossible to get help and equally impossible to hold the help once they get it. There is nothing to hinder a neighbour from climbing the line fence and saying to a farm labourer-I know of instances of this-"You are doing a good job ploughing; how much are you getting?" The man might reply, "$55 and my board." "All right, come down the line and I will give you $60; my credit is a little better; where are you from?" "Saskatchewan." "The last man was from there and I understand he did not get his money." That is what happens. The man goes down to the next place, and the man on the next farm does the same thing.
They are used to not getting their money in Saskatchewan.

I do not want to reflect upon Saskatchewan. Many healthy fellows come from there. I have given much thought as has every person who has had anything to do with agriculture, to this matter of farm labour. Whether it be popular or unpopular I want to say that I do not believe in this price freezing of farm products, in setting price ceilings. I do not think it can be applied to agricultural production with success, even as a war time measure.
We are freezing the wages paid to our labouring men and giving them a cost of living bonus as well. Why are we paying a cost of living bonus? We are paying this to protect the labouring men against a rise in the cost of primary products, against rise in the cost of foodstuffs. When the Minister of Agriculture is fixing the price of butter at thirty seven cents a pound he does not know whether I shall have to pay $5 a day for labour, or whether the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) will have to pay $6 a day because he happens to be nearer to a factory. When men are able to go home and still work in a factory, the factory offers strong competition for farm labour. The farmer is not only unable to get sufficient help, but must pay a wage rate twice what it was in 1939.
I am not for one moment claiming that these men are getting more than they should. Even now they are not getting as much as the man with similar ability and initiative is being paid in industry. I have always felt that we shall never have a well organized

prosperity in this country until the farm labourer is placed on an equality with the industrial labourer. The farm labourer is entitled to a fair price for his toil. He should not be asked to work longer hours for shorter pay. I hope the day is coming when the farmer will receive the same for eight hours labour on the farm as is paid to the industrial worker for eight hours labour in the factory. The farm labourer has not reached that point even though he may be receiving twice as much as he received before the government tried in the summer time to fix the wintertime prices of the commodities produced by the farmer.
It is all very well to tell the farmer that he is a great fellow, that he is the backbone of the country, that what he does is just as important as what the soldier in the front line is doing. I know however, that the boy on the farm cannot satisfy his own conscience and feel that he is writing as much on the pages of history when he is standing behind a plough as his brother behind a machine gun. I cannot convince myself that the boy on the farm is as proud and as satisfied with the service he is giving, even though he may be keeping a widowed mother. He feels that service overseas, while more dangerous, is more glorious.
If we are to produce to the limit from the great agricultural resources of this dominion, this government must stop, look and listen. It must realize what is happening. Thousands of acres in western Ontario, thousands of acres in Simcoe county, thousands of acres in Duf-ferin county, thousands of acres in the county of the Postmaster General, York county, are idle to-day. They are idle because of the uncertainty as to what is to be paid for the products which can be raised on the farm. Ceilings are being placed upon what the farmer has to sell, and floors are being placed on what he has to buy. That is not sound economy. It will retard the production that we should be developing.
It is all very well to read a bulletin and say that we have produced much more this year than we did last year; it is all very well to say that we are getting higher prices, but I do not hear anyone say that the farmer is forced to pay twice as much in wages. I do not hear the Minister of Labour assuring us that these wages will be fixed for next year and that a cost of living bonus will be provided. I cannot hear anyone assuring me as to what I shall have to pay for harvest labour.
I am doubtful about the whole price-ceiling scheme and its effect upon our economic picture. The old law of supply and demand should

War Appropriation-Agriculture
be given more freedom, and it must be given more freedom if we are to meet the demand by an accelerated supply. The farmer is the forgotten man and has been placed in a most ridiculous position. The government praises him for his loyalty and coaxes him to produce for less; it tells him that his products are as important as bullets, and at the same time it tells him that it is going to put a ceiling on what he has to sell and a floor on what he has to buy. The government will not tell him what he will get next year for his products, but it gives him soya beans to sow and tells him that he will not get more than $1.95 a bushel.
We guarantee him

It is all very well to talk
about where prices went in the last war. I am of opinion that the rise in prices which occurred in the last war had more to d'o with keeping our troops from starving than any other single thing. Not only the soldiers but the whole of Europe will be pleading for foodstuffs. I realize, of course, the shortage of shipping, but after the war, all of Europe will be needing our foodstuffs.
At the present time we are giving the farmer only about 20 to 25 per cent more for his butter than he received when he was paying 100 per cent less in wages, and yet when he goes into town he is told he had better eat one piece of butter instead of two. The same is true of agricultural prices all down the line.
With reference to bacon production-let me say incidentally that I have not eaten a pound of bacon in the last two months, thinking it was loyal to refrain-I am to-day producing bacon for only about- 25 per cent more than I got when I was paying 100 per cent less in wages. In this connection I would urge the minister to raise the weight of hogs fifty pounds each. Let the farmers produce, not a 185-pound hog, but a 225-pound hog as we did in the last war.

That is what they are
now, 185 pounds dressed, 225 pounds on foot.

Make it 225 pounds dressed.
May I say that I was docked one dollar the other day because my hogs were one pound overweight. These long, stream-lined, white Yorkshire hogs that we were urged to raise so that our bacon could compete on the British breakfast table with the lean bacon from Denmark, so that the girl who was tripping off to her office and wanted to keep her girlish figure would not have to eat too much fat, is not the size of hog we should be raising to-day. What we want now is more fats and more oils and more bulk. These
long, thin hogs can carry fifty pounds more weight, and1 the boys overseas and the starving people over there would rather have their bacon with a little fat on it than half as much pork with no fat at all. It is true that Denmark is now out of the picture. We might have to revert to the better grades to meet post-war competition, but what is wanted to-day is foodstuffs for an emergency, fats for a crisis, not stream-lined bacon for the woman who is working only a few hours a day.

And who
is thinking of a fashionable figure.

Exactly. I urge the minister
to set aside for the time being these restrictive regulations which have only proved unprofitable and confusing to the farmer, and let him produce a hog weighing fifty more pounds. That would increase our production by hundreds of millions of pounds.
I urge the minister and his government to give consideration to the position in which agriculture in this country finds itself to-day. It has never been so confusing to the farmer. Never has there been so much uncertainty ahead of him, and never has he had a more important task to perform. Particularly do I urge this upon the minister now that the farmer has to pay 100 per cent more in wages and there is a ceiling on his products. What we should be doing is to put a floor on his products. Try giving him a fair price rather than a fixed price. I am not suggesting that our farmers want bacon to go up to $26 per 100 pounds or butter to 90 cents a pound or eggs to $1 a dozen. I know that within two miles of my home a farmer sold 100 good laying hens last winter because he would not produce eggs in winter at summer-time prices. He started in the business with the intention of having 2,000 or 3,000 hens, and he sold when he had 800 hens. Another neighbour with 300 hens sold all but fifty for the same reason. I said to one of these men, "Why don't you wait? The government is struggling with price ceilings, and there will be a demand for eggs. They are needed for war purposes." But he replied, "It is all too uncertain. If the government is going to fix a price where there is practically no profit in it for us, and adopt that as a policy, when we do not know what we shall have to pay in wages for help which I shall have to hire because our boys are gone to the war, I am better off without the hens." That is the position of agriculture all along the line. The government has no agricultural policy. I realize that they are confused, that they are trying to get out of a crisis, that they are trying to coordinate agricultural production with this novel price-ceiling policy. I realize the difficulties involved; but



War Appropriation-Agriculture
I would say, in conclusion, that you cannot fix a price ceiling on what an industry has to sell and a floor price only on what it has to buy.

I want to congratulate the previous speaker. It is the first time I have really agreed with him in this house. I do not think that is an unfair remark. We are on opposite sides of politics, but his was a good speech all round.
You are fair.

I try to be, and I try to pick up information as I go along. I have often wondered what the streamlined type was, but after hearing the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe, I know now that it is a hog from Toronto.
The Minister of Agriculture said some time ago that farm labour came under the Minister of Labour and that the wartime prices and trade board came under the Minister of Finance. I want to quote what the Minister of Finance said as reported at page 2909 of Hansard. Among other things he said:
The subsidy was discontinued on May 1st, because effective on that date the board established a new scale of maximum milk prices and made provision for other adjustments in milk production practices, so that adequate prices may be paid to producers to enable them to continue production.
The Minister of Agriculture says that we must go to the Minister of Labour in connection with hours of labour, and that we must go to the Minister of Finance in connection with the wartime prices and trade board. I do not know how we can approach this question except through our Minister of Agriculture. We who come from agricultural ridings look to the Minister of Agriculture to do that very thing for us. I am inclined to agree with the last speaker; I have no more desire than anybody else to see inflation, but I think it is obvious that the last man to be hurt in Canada or in any other country by inflation is the farmer.
I consider it to be the duty of the Minister of Agriculture, on behalf of and representing a rural riding, to see that it is brought home to the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance that we simply cannot continue to exist under the present financial and labour set-up. In British Columbia for the past two months dairy cattle have been disposed of at the average rate of a sale and a half a day. These dairy cattle, the finest we have in Canada, are being slaughtered for beef purposes because we cannot get milkers and other labour.
I am not contending that farm labourers receive too much. Nor can one blame any farmer's son or other working men for taking 
advantage of the high rates of wages in war industries. To my way of thinking, however, the Department of Agriculture should formulate some scheme, either of bonusing farm labour or seeing to it that the wartime prices and trade board allows us a sufficient price for farm produce to permit of our paying adequate wages to keep the men on the farms. It is not at all to the credit of one of the greatest agricultural countries in the world that our dairy cattle are being slaughtered for beef at the present time, and I think it is a condition which could easily be overcome-though here my hon. friends to the left will probably claim all the credit for the suggestion-by a little planned economy. Surely we can plan ahead a little bit. If we had adopted some system of planning our labour supply a few years ago, we would not have the condition that is existing on the farms to-day.
However, I am not quarrelling about that, but I am definitely objecting to what in my opinion has happened as regards setting the price of milk. It has been set on a cheese basis. I do not know the reason for that, but I venture the statement that no practical dairy man, unless he is also in the cheese business, is sitting on any of the wartime prices boards. It is obvious that if it is made so much more advantageous to produce cheese, there is going to be a reduction in our other dairy products. In the Fraser valley, where I come from 75 per cent of our milk is marketed throughout the largest cooperative dairy association in Canada. I am not exaggerating; the minister knows it is true. He may not know that there are only two larger dairy cooperatives on the north American continent. It is a very large organization. We sell on consignment 75 per cent of the milk produced in the Fraser valley, which practically means it is the milkshed of British Columbia. Of that, only 25 per cent goes on to the fluid market. Anyone who knows anything about dairying knows that his money comes from the fluid market. The wartime prices and trade board were going to permit us in Vancouver to increase the retail price of our milk one cent, on the 1st of May. Our settling rate was fifty cents a pound butterfat. If we took advantage of that, the price would be approximately sixty cents a pound butterfat; but if you follow it through, although we handle 75 per cent of the milk, only 25 per cent of it is fluid milk. We stand to gain two cents a pound butterfat as regards the 75 per cent of total production; but our competitors, who market 75 per cent of their

25 per cent on the fluidi market, will gain seven and a half cents. I do not think the minister's department intended anything like that.
In my opinion, the sooner agriculture gets back under the Department of Agriculture and away from some of these wartime boards, the better for agriculture. I believe the minister will be fair enough to admit that he has not any more control over agriculture in the Dominion of Canada to-day than I, as a private member, have. Some dollar-a-year man or some such other unnecessary "critter on these boards controls the price the farmer is to get. The minister cannot deny that.

Not while the hon.
member is speaking.

I am not depreciating the minister's value, because I can say-and this is one way to say it safely and keep the friendship of my friends,-that there is only one other man in the House of Commons who I believe is capable of filling his shoes, and I am not going to say who that is.

The hon.
member is too modest.

There will be
plenty of applications; I know that. I am not going any further into the labour problem, but I believe the fact has been overlooked that everything the farmer uses and must use in his normal production has increased in price to a great extent, in some instances by 100 per cent. Take one so-called tool of the farmer, with the use of which some of these legal-minded farmers are probably not very familiar, at any rate since their youth-the manure fork. At the beginning of the war it cost $1.15; now it costs $1.95. But the price of milk and other products has not risen correspondingly. Potatoes rotted in the pits in British Columbia this year. I know it is very easy to criticize and to declare what the minister should do and what he should not do. But there is one suggestion I might make as far as my own province is concerned, and I think it affects parts of Ontario, certainly the city of Ottawa. On any street here where there is an apartment building you will find ten or fifteen or sometimes twenty milk trucks or carts delivering milk and cream to that building. There is one place that the minister might act, if he has any control over this agricultural set-up. At least he could write a letter to one of these boards and tell them to do something. They could dispense with many of these trucks by some system of consolidation of deliveries.
Some of the dollar-ayear men are doing that now.

Well, as usual, and as I have heard from my hon. friends on the left, they are doing it at the rate at which we are accused of carrying on the war effort; they are extremely slow about it. There is no question about that. I am afraid that the hon. member who has just spoken is never up early enough in the morning, unless he is going home, to know what is going on. If he would come around to-morrow morning I could show him places in the city of Ottawa where there are ten trucks delivering at one apartment building. That could be avoided by a system of consolidated deliveries of milk and other products.
There is another way in which I think we could assist the dairyman; it was touched on briefly by the hon. member for New Westminster. I am glad to hear the minister say that it is under consideration, and I am going to take it for granted that it is as good as accomplished, because when the minister puts his mind to anything he generally gets his own way.

He is
having an awful struggle now with Mr. Gordon.

To continue this freight rate system will assist the dairymen considerably. It would also assist us in connection with our dairy production if the minister would see to it that the rural ridings get a fair deal on this system of gasoline rationing. I know it is not his branch, but as a rural member I deem it my duty to look to my Minister of Agriculture. He is the kingpin in the agricultural industry in so far as this parliament is concerned, and it should be his privilege as well as his duty to represent us in every way. As regards gasoline, the first man the wartime prices and trade board picked on was the farmer. They allowed the brewery salesman to go round with category C, but the farmer, whether handling dairy products or nursery stock or any other line, gets only category A. Probably hon. members do not know that. I think a considerable saving could be effected along that line.
The brewery industry has a doilar-a-year representative here.
I think he comes from the maritimes too.

There is another matter I would bring to the attention of the minister because I have received a letter in connection with it. I think the minister will admit that it must be hard on the farmer in the Fraser valley, working from five o'clock in the morning to half-past eight at night, to obtain, as this particular man did last month, 100 pounds of 4 per cent milk. A good many members here will say, "I was brought up on a farm and I love the land." Yes, but as soon as they get an opportunity to move away from the land they take advantage of it. I wonder how many members know how much milking one has to do to get 100 pounds of 4 per cent milk, and then he gets exactly SI.66 net for it on the farm. Is it any wonder that these people write to me or even borrow the money to pay for a telegram. In these days of speedy travel they can get newspaper pictures out west very quickly. Four days ago there appeared in the newspapers the picture of a handsome young man. He was really a fine looking fellow; indeed, I thought he was a moving-picture actor. As I say, he was young too. Well, to my surprise he was not overseas, under the splendid selective draft system which we have. No; he was an artist. Will anyone tell me, when there is a war on, and farmers are getting $1.66 for 100 pounds of 4 per cent milk, what on earth we need an artist for in the department? It does not make sense. I suggest this is one direction in which economy could be effected. Why do we want an artist working in connection with entomology; we have enough bugs without this man. If it is the intention of the department to let the dairy industry in the Fraser valley fall by the wayside, very well; they are proceeding in the right way. If, however, they want to maintain the dairy industry, then I suggest that they adopt a different attitude. There is no question about that. When auction sales are taking place continually in an area eighty miles long by thirty miles wide, an average of one and a half sales a day, at which the finest dairy cattle in Canada are disposed of, it will be realized that we are not doing anything to save the dairy industry. There are men who have been in that industry for fifty and sixty years, born and brought up in it, and yet they are selling every one of their cattle. In the face of such a situation, neither the department nor the government nor this parliament has anything to be proud of in the manner in which dairy farming has been handled in Canada.
Is that taking place now?

Absolutely; there is no doubt about it. All one has to do is look up the local papers in British Columbia and see the list of advertisements or go through the valley himself and see what is taking place. I am not suggesting that the farm labourer is getting too much money. In my riding they are receiving, in some instances, from $80 to $125 a month and board for milking. Well, one cannot pay such wages at the price of dairy products. Last month when they were getting $1.66 per 100 pounds of four per cent milk, day labour was receiving $3.60-and I am not quarrelling over the fact that the day labourer receives that amount. Probably they should get more. At any rate, they were getting $3.60; and if the farmer produced 200 pounds of milk and had a man working for him, he lost twenty-eight cents on the operation. That sort of thing cannot continue, and yet no effort is being made to alleviate the situation.
I suggest that the government should do something in regard to farmers' sons.

Some hon. gentlemen call me to order when I interrupt the member for Temiscouata, but they do not call anyone to order for interrupting me. In British Columbia, at least as far as my riding is concerned, we have never applied for exemptions for farmers' sons. I have never recommended a solitary one, because I do not believe in that sort of thing. I do not believe it is the prerogative of a member of parliament to do so. At the same time I submit that more consideration should be given to any bona fide farmer's son so as to allow him to stay on the farm. Here may I pay a little tribute to the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore). I suggest that sometimes, if we paid a little more attention to what he says, we might gain a little knowledge. I am not referring to his monetary system, because I understand neither his system nor the old one; but if we had given more attention to him we as a parliament- since I have been here at any rate-might have learned enough to wake up to a realization of the sugar beet situation. What is happening now? We are rationed on sugar because we were not longsighted enough to go in for the production of sugar beets.
The story has already been told by previous speakers with regard to labour, but it is the duty of the minister to impress upon the wartime prices and trade board the importance of this question. If he were free to tell us what he thinks of the board, he and I might agree. At any rate, we cannot continue

War Appropriation-Agriculture
production in British Columbia if conditions remain as they are. I do not profess to be speaking with full authority for my constituents, but I am certainly expressing my own opinion when I say that it is doubtful whether the price ceiling is of any material benefit to agriculture. I doubt very much if it is. I think it is a detriment.
It is a detriment.

In my opinion it is. We are being penalized; the forgotten man is being penalized for the benefit of the rest of Canada as a whole. If we are to be penalized-possibly it may be for the good of the country in the long run-surely we should receive something to compensate us in that regard, so that the farmer may be allowed to carry on. There should be an ample subsidy, or he should be given a guaranteed price for his product. The manufacturer is guaranteed a profit on what he produces. I do not say he should not have that guarantee, but there is not a shell manufactured or any other manufactured article produced in Canada on which the manufacturer does not know in advance what his profit will be. On the other hand, there is not a solitary article produced by the farmer of which this can be said. The farmer does not know, before he produces it, what profit he will get on anything he produces. I am not saying that there are not certain articles produced by farmers on which a profit is made, but the producer does not know that beforehand, as the minister admitted in connection with poultry and potatoes. The producer does not know until after he has produced the cpmmodity. How many tanks or planes should we get produced at a loss if we said, "produce for victory, for patriotic purposes?" We would not get a wheelbarrow produced by that gang in Quebec and Toronto if we asked them to produce for patriotic purposes. We must be realistic; the farmers must be guaranteed a fair return for the energy and money invested.
I was not quite sure whether the hon. member said most of those dairy herds were being sold for slaughter.

I would not say most of them. We found that there were auction sales at the rate of one and a half a day. We checked on one sale of splendid dairy cattle and found that within forty-eight hours 98 per cent of two herds were slaughtered in Vancouver.

It is not my intention to argue the pros and cons regarding the wartime prices and trade board, nor do I wish to suggest that the price of cheese has been set too high. What I do say is that when the price of cheese was set the price of other dairy products was set too low. In other words, the butter price was set too low. One product of the dairy industry which I have not heard mentioned is condensed milk. At one time the constituency which I have the honour to represent was the greatest cheese-producing county in Canada. To-day we are one of the large cheese-producing counties. A great deal of the milk that formerly went into the production of cheese is now going into condensed and evaporated milk. In fact the farmers have become largely dependent on that outlet for the sale of their milk.
As matters now stand, the price for condensed milk has been set so low that the companies cannot meet the price paid by the cheese factories. Although I understand the minister's hands are tied by the wartime prices and trade board I should like to inquire whether there is any possibility of having the condensed milk business bonused as are a great many other industries. It is a very grave question with us. Even if the farmers should decide to stop selling to the condenseries, I am afraid they would be out of luck inasmuch as a great many cheese factories have gone out of business; some have been burnt; some have fallen into disrepair; others have actually had their machinery sold. As yet the condenseries are meeting almost the prices paid by the cheese factories; but this cannot go on, and in justice to our farmers some system must be worked out whereby it will be as profitable to sell milk to a condensery as to sell it either as fluid milk to a dairy or to a cheese factory. Even at the present cheese price the farmer is not getting what he should for his milk, although it is far better than it was. I cannot understand the prices quoted by the hon. member for Fraser Valley. Fortunately milk prices in eastern Canada are considerably higher than that, even if a bonus has to be paid in certain instances. One assurance that must be given-and I was glad to hear the Minister of Agriculture saying that consideration is now being given to the matter of freight rates on coarse grains to the'Pacific coast and the east-the farmers must be guaranteed a continuation of reasonably stable prices on feeds. Otherwise I can visualize a condition in this section of Canada such as seems to prevail in the Fraser valley. We are losing a great many of our high-grade registered cattle, not for slaughter purposes I am happy to say, but buyers from the United
War Appropriation-Agriculture

States are coming into Canada in large numbers and buying the very choicest cattle in our herds.
At high prices.
A dangerous situation.

It is. The prices are high but not too high. I am not arguing that point. I am glad that for once the farmers are receiving something, but to me it is a serious matter that the very cream of our herds is being exported to the United States. Something must be done to keep these fine cattle in Canada. If they are not kept we shall be left with the stragglers, the poorest type. Before the war it was possible to import stock from Guernsey, Jersey, Schleswig-Holstein, but we do not know what the Germans have done to those cattle. We must keep our stock up to the highest possible level, and the only way I can see to do it is for the government to formulate a definite policy, bonusing the farmers if you will, to keep their herds at the highest possible level of quality.
I sincerely hope that the Minister of Agriculture can persuade the wartime prices and trade board either to raise the prices of butter and condensed milk or to pay a bonus so that the dairy industry will be once more equalized and not in a state of constant flux as it is to-day.

Why is there a disparity between cheese and butter prices? This afternoon the hon. member for New Westminster said that cheese products were in the ratio of fifty, as compared with thirty-five for butter. Throughout the country people who are in a position to deliver their milk products to cheese factories claim they are making better money than those who make deliveries to creameries. In my province and, I suppose throughout the prairie provinces generally, we have scarcely any cheese factories. Indeed, under the system of priorities it would be difficult to have cheese factories constructed in that area. I am wondering if the dairy products board could not guarantee to the dairy producers the same price for their butter fat, whether it is used for cheese or butter or whole milk. In my view the present position is discriminatory and I suggest that the minister should give some concrete explanation for this condition.

I suggest that the board should be instructed to pay these producers on a basis of equality for butter fat. Would the minister suggest that the board might do that?

I did give a partial explanation this afternoon. The explanation is provided not so much by the Department of Agriculture as on behalf of those who are establishing ceiling prices in Canada. The suggestion is that we can increase butter production by having a higher price during the winter months, rather than in the summer. That is one suggestion. The real reason for any disparity between prices of cheese and butter since the beginning of the war is that Britain desires cheese. Year after year she has been urging us to produce the greatest possible quantity of Canadian Cheddar cheese to be shipped to Great Britain. Last year we suggested that all we thought we would be able to get under the conditions then existing was about 112,000,000 pounds. We just managed to get that amount by refusing to permit the sale of any Canadian cheese in Canada. Cheese made between May 26 and October 1 of last year was all shipped to Great Britain; none of it was allowed to be sold in Canada. During the winter months we allowed a higher price, and did get a very considerable production of cheese in those months. It is argued that by the plan which is now being followed of having a thirty-five-cent ceiling in the summer months and a higher ceiling in the winter months we can get a considerable production of butter in the winter months of the coming year.
I said this afternoon I was not at all sure as to whether the results would be what are expected. Nevertheless that is being tried out for the time being, and we are cooperating in every possible way to bring about a favourable result. The suggestion was made this afternoon that a price of fifty cents for butter would compare favourably with the present price of cheese. But one would have to include with the price of cheese the subsidies paid by provincial governments and the premium paid by the federal government in order to raise the comparable butter price to that level.
The price paid for cheese exported to Great Britain is twenty cents a pound. We have always considered that two cents for butter to one for cheese would be about the proper relationship. Based on the actual price that would mean about forty cents a pound for butter. There has been a demand made to keep the price as nearly as possible at proportionate levels. The argument is put forth at the present that we may get all the

War Appropriation-Agriculture
butter production we require, and at the same time encourage a greater production of cheese for Great Britain by having the present disparity in prices.

There is no great surplus of butter, is there? I read that there may be a shortage of butter. If there is no great surplus, I should think the argument should prevail that there should be as nearly as possible a parity on all dairy products.

I think one hon. member this afternoon used the correct figure when he said that storages were down about 5,000,000 pounds at the beginning of last month, as compared with a year ago. If nothing else is taken into consideration, this indicates that there might be a shortage of butter at the end of this season. We have been accustomed to expect our peak production in May and June, the production then tapering off in July, and still further in August and September. This year it is hoped we shall have increased production next winter, with the higher prices, in order to make up for anything which drops off during the factory cheese producing months this summer.
I should add that we are hopeful at this time of being able to get the 125,000,000 pounds of cheese we have agreed to send to Britain; but we are not yet in a position to state with any assurance that we shall have the full amount of butter which will be required for consumption in Canada.

I was interested this
afternoon to hear the Minister of Agriculture talking about butter and cheese. I have been in that business for about forty years and, although I am not an expert, I believe I know something about the industry. It would seem that the minister and his advisers are a little worried that we may run short of butter this year. The fiscal year, if I may so describe it, for cheese and butter, is from the first of May to the last of April in the following year. Last year we received 85,000 boxes of butter as compared with 50,000 boxes received this year. On the other hand, we received this year 150,000 boxes of cheese as compared with 50,000 boxes last year. There is no necessity for an expert to see at once that we are going to run short of butter before the year is over. Unless we can import some butter I would urge the minister to give serious consideration to the situation and not to wait until the first of October before he revises 'his plans. I know that after the first of October very little milk is produced, and unless a very high price is paid for butter, he wiU not get it at all.
I do not make this suggestion to embarrass the minister, because I always pity ministers when they are being grilled with respect to their estimates-although I know that the passage of estimates is almost a holiday for the present Minister of Agriculture. I do not believe any more milk will be produced this year than last because there is a scarcity of labour. Farmers' sons have been enlisting, and others have been drafted. Many farmers are reducing their herds. They cannot hire help; that is out of the question. The result is that for many reasons we shall be short of butter, because at this time there is a better market for whole milk, condensed milk and cheese. Consequently, if the production of milk is the same as it was last year we cannot expect any increased production. Last fall we had about 8,000,000 pounds of butter that we did not know what to do with, but the purchasing power of our people increased to such an extent that that butter disappeared diuring the winter and was practically all gone on May 1. This year we should have a greater production because we have the market for it.
I do not know that the minister can do much about this matter because we have the wartime prices and trade board. I wonder if that board knows anything about cattle. I wonder if it knows which end of a cow should be milked. I think the government whenever possible should take the advice of those who know something about this business. The other night the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann) complained about not being appointed to committees where his advice on medical matters might be of value. I urge the minister to consider these suggestions carefully. I know he is a good listener. About a week ago I wrote him to urge that the butter fat content of ice cream be cut down in order to conserve butter fat. Before I received an answer an order in council was passed reducing the butter fat content to where I wanted it. I compliment the minister upon that action.

This afternoon the hon.
member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) wanted to know why the price of milk was always tied up to the price of cheese. The reason is that that is usually the lowest price paid for milk. At the present time a controversy is going on with regard to condensed or powdered milk manufactured in this country. The milk board of Ontario has set the price at 81.95 per 100 pounds for 3-5 per cent milk. That is 25 cents per 100 pounds above what the basic price had been for some time. In April the cheese factories paid $1.50 per 100 pounds or 47 cents a pound butter

War Appropriation-Agriculture
fat for 3-2 per cent milk. How can a farmer who must sell his milk to the butter factory continue in business when he receives only 35 cents a pound butter fat? There is a difference of 12 cents a pound between the price paid for milk to be manufactured into cheese, and that paid for milk to be manufactured into butter. There is a greater discrimination in connection with milk going to the condenser or powdered milk plants.
It is necessary that a great part of our milk should go into the production of cheese because we must produce 125,000,000 pounds during this year if we are to fulfil our agreement with Great Britain. I have no doubt that this will be done; in fact, our production may be greater than that if there is some coordination and control over the milk industry. The Minister of Finance is in his place, and I understand that the payment of subsidies comes under his department. I should like to draw something to his attention as well as to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture. Last December the farmer was selling his milk to the cheese factory when cheese at 25 cents a pound had the advantage, but the farmer who was sending milk to the condenser or powdered milk plant suffered to the extent of at least 40 cents per 100 pounds of milk, as at that time the ceiling on cheese allowed a price higher than the price being paid by the condenseries.
In April last the cheese factories were paying at the rate of $1.50 per 100 pounds for 3-2 per cent milk, or 47 cents a pound butter fat. At this time the basic price at the condenser for 3-5 per cent milk was $1.70 per 100 pounds. There was 40 cents per 100 pounds subsidy paid by the federal government, which brought this amount up to $2.10 per 100 pounds. I have a suggestion to make which might help to overcome the discrimination in favour of the man sending milk to the condenser or powdered milk plant. There should be coordination and control by the dairy products board so that each farmer will get approximately the same return for his milk. The flow of milk will always be to the point at which the highest price is paid, but this board should be given power to control and allot milk to the cheese factories in sufficient quantity to produce the 125,000,000 pounds of cheese required by the British government. Then the remainder could be allotted to the condensers and powdered milk plants. I understand there is a considerable demand overseas for condensed milk. The rest of the milk production could be allowed to go into butter channels. By the exercise of this control each and every farmer would get approximately the same return for his labour.

It looked as though the Minister of Agriculture had made a good bargain with the British government when he was able to get 20 cents a pound for our cheese. In April last, however, there was not much cheese shipped to Great Britain out of the make priced at $1.50 per 100 pounds for 3-2 per cent milk. That includes the premium paid by the federal government as well as the 2 cents a pound paid by Ontario. That did not give a large return to the farmer especially when one takes into account-this has been referred to so many times-his extra cost of labour and the extra cost of those commodities he must purchase. It is not in any way a parity price. I believe a great service could be rendered by the government of Canada by empowering the dairy products board to coordinate the supply of milk going into manufacturing purposes of all kinds.

I should like to support what has been said by the hon. member for Shefford. The outlook is not very promising for an increase in the production of butter. I do not think it is wise to wait until October to make this experiment, as the minister suggested to-day. I would ask the minister whether he does not think a slight increase in the price of butter fat would improve the situation. Over the week-endi I talked with people who manufacture butter and cheese in my constituency, and I find that they are paying thirty-eight cents a pound for butter fat which is used in the manufacture of butter, and fifty cents a pound for butter fat used in the manufacture of cheese. A five-cent increase in the price would bring the price of butter fat for making butter to forty-one or forty-two cents a pound. There are a great many farmers who consider that the skim-milk which is left is an asset that is worth something to them, and so in my opinion if that slight increase of five cents a pound for butter fat used in the manufacture of butter were made, it would divert to the butter factory some of the milk that is now going to the cheese factory. If, however, we wait until next October before we do anything, conditions are not going to improve.
In the break-down which was put on Hansard by the Minister of Finance I noticed an item of $1,514,950 for the dairy products board. I can recall when this butter and cheese question was up two years ago and the suggestion was made that there should be a dairy products board to regulate the production of butter and cheese, to keep the two commodities on an even keel, so that it would not be necessary to divert the butter fat from one product to the other. But now we are right back to

War Appropriation-Agriculture
where we were; only the picture is the reverse. We have plenty of cheese now, and not enough butter.
I would think the dairy products board could control to a certain extent the production of these two commodities, butter and cheese, and keep them on an even keel, and I believe the speaker who preceded me had the same thought in mind, so that it would not be necessary to be continually diverting butter fat from one product to the other. I should like to hear from the minister whether he thinks an increase in the price of butter fat would make some improvement at the present time.

I agree with the two
speakers who have preceded me. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox is very good with regard to stabilizing the price of dairy products right across the dominion. We in western Canada have been trying for the last several years to get away from straight wheat farming into mixed farming. There has been a greater percentage of increase in the quantity of dairy products produced in the west in the last few years than anywhere else in the dominion; and yet to-day we are receiving in my home town only thirty-three cents a pound for butter fat, whereas producers in other parts of the dominion are receiving approximately fifty cents a pound. That is too great a spread, and the result will be to discourage dairying in western Canada, where I believe it should be increased.
The marketing board should take under consideration the advisability of adjusting the price of dairy products across the dominion. Prices could not be exactly alike all over; there would probably be a differential between different districts, but there is no justification for that great spread of from thirty-five to forty per cent between the price paid to-day in western Canada and that paid in other parts of the dominion. Producers of butter fat in other parts of the dominion are receiving a certain adjustment with regard to freight rates on feed grain, and I believe that is all to the good. That is a very good policy and it should be continued. At the same time there- should be greater equality in the price of dairy products as between different parts of this dominion and different types of production, and that is particularly necessary at this time if we are to have increased production.

I was very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Davidson) who, if the facts were known to. all members of the
house, is, next to the breeders in the county of Peel, one of the largest Jersey breeders we have in eastern Canada. I know he will not think I am reflecting on him when I place those in the county of Peel a little ahead.
A discussion of agriculture under this war appropriation measure, and in its relation to our general war effort, is very much to be desired at this time, because it is impossible, as I see it, to visualize the broad scheme of the nation's war effort without bringing into the picture very solidly, firmly and in a conspicuous position agriculture's share in the supplying of food.
The position of agriculture in Canada upon the outbreak of hostilities left a good deal to be desired. Even during the period of the war agriculture has felt, and justifiably so, I think, that its position in relation to that of other industries more closely related to the war effort and to others not as closely related has not reached parity; in other words, agriculture has not been getting a fair return or its fair share of the national income. Those views have been advanced on a great many occasions, and I have no desire to-night to do more than simply reemphasize what has been so well said on previous occasions.
During the last few weeks, in addition to the great delegation which came from western Canada to Ottawa asking, not for concessions because they would not call them that, but that the rightful position of agriculture in the general economy and in relation to the war effort should be recognized, another important group made representations to the government of Canada, and many of us who represent rural constituencies in Ontario were privileged to sit in at that gathering. That was when the agricultural council of Ontario came, representing, as hon. members who are familiar with its activities know, many of those who are prominent in the agricultural and municipal life of the province. They presented several resolutions to the government, and I think members of parliament could very well take a leaf out of the book of these farmers for the brevity and clarity and orderly way in which they marshalled their arguments from beginning to end. I believe the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Finance will agree with me when I say that within the short space of an hour and a quarter the whole argument on the five resolutions had been well and truly presented to the government by the agricultural council, and they were highly complimented upon their presentation.
War Appropriation-Agriculture

I have no intention to-night of dealing with all the resolutions they presented, but I should like to touch on one or two which have particular merit with respect to the present situation. One was this; and while the Minister of Agriculture may be able to say that this is a matter not completely within the scope and sphere of his department, I believe he has a wide influence in the cabinet, and I hope, indeed I know, that he will use it to have this rectified and remedied. Many farmers during this war-time period have had to change in many respects their style of operation. The fact is that, as most rural members realize, farm help is not only a matter of wages; you cannot get experienced help in a good many areas no matter what you pay. That being so, the farmer has had to turn, where he could, to an increased use of machinery. In my own county a considerable number of milking machines have been installed since the war began. The reeve of one of the municipalities in my constituency, speaking on behalf of the agricultural council when they met here two or three weeks ago, stated that he had increased his flow of whole milk for the Toronto market some 30 per cent by installing milking machines and using less farm labour.
That being so, the supply of electrical equipment and power comes in a very important manner into the picture. In many instances the farmer, in attempting to put in a milking machine, a cooler, or some other modem machinery or equipment so essential in these days to the whole milk trade in that particular area, finds that, even where a hydroelectric line passes right by his gate and it is only a matter of bringing the power in from the gate to his stable or other buildings, one of the government boards which are so popular with the hon. member for Fraser Valley, in exercising its authority with regard to steel and power control, will not make the necessary power available. So the farmer, even though help is so scarce, has this obstacle, though perhaps inadvertently, placed in his way at a time when he requires extra machinery to carry on; all this by virtue of the regulation of some board which, I quite believe, has not one farmer on it. The orders of the power controller are affecting very many farmers in Ontario. Perhaps I should not mention figures, but there are dozens of farmers in the area from which I come who have been trying for a considerable time to obtain permission from the controller to get electric current just from the roadway into their bams. Some of them have even the equipment but cannot connect up with the current. I am not suggesting that the Minister of Agriculture is 
responsible, because he is not, but I would like to see him take, in this connection, the aggressive stand which he does on many other matters, and see that some concession is made to the farmer who is attempting to substitute farm machinery for the human help he cannot get at this time. It is not impossible, I am told, for those in residential sections in urban centres to get some types of installation, even to-day; and since this equipment is part of the tools of the farmer in his business, he ought in fairness to be able to install power machinery which means so much to the operation of his farm.
I have said on a previous occasion, but I want to stress the point again, that before we go much further in this war effort I believe we are going to suffer a grave and acute shortage of agricultural supplies. The minister and the government have been somewhat remiss in not exercising the foresight to plan for agricultural supplies in the same manner as they have planned for other types of wartime production and activity. I know it is not always easy to foresee future trends as regards farm products; but even to the average layman it must be abundantly clear that, if farm help continues to be hard to get, if as many farmers are holding sales as we were told this afternoon are being held in the Fraser valley, and if so many are going into other types of industry as we have been told repeatedly in this chamber is a fact, only one result can follow, having regard to the fact that there is more demand for agricultural products than there was when we had a greater number of farmers and more help to man the farms. I would therefore suggest to the minister that this government should at once give deep and serious consideration to planning its agricultural policy with a view of avoiding and averting what I think will otherwise be a grave shortage of farm products and farm supplies within the next year, if this war continues at its present tempo.
Some reference has been made to the whole milk industry. Perhaps it does not cover as wide a territory geographically as that of some other lines of dairy production which have been mentioned here to-day, but it is a tremendous industry and, with respect to the metropolitan area of Toronto has been-

I wonder if hon. members would agree with me if I were to say that since the dinner recess we have been discussing the dairy products board and its activities, which we had agreed before the dinner recess we would leave until we were dealing with the last five items. Could we not clear up the general remarks with regard to agriculture which were to come in on the

War Appropriation-Agriculture
above items? Up to the moment the hon. member has been dealing with the general items, but it appears that now he is going into the matter of the dairy products board. Perhaps he would confine the discussion to the upper items, and we can deal with the other items when we come to them.

Yes. Unfortunately I
was not in the chamber when the arrangement was made, and I apologize to the minister. I should like to continue my remarks when we come to the dairy products board item, because there are one or two observations I wish to make.

I notice in the war appropriation estimates before us an item of $230,000 for "programmes to encourage the production of essential war supplies." In view of the foresight which the Minister of Agriculture has shown and is showing, it is quite possible that what I am about to say may be like carrying coals to Newcastle. But I wonder whether the minister has, in collaboration with his colleagues, canvassed the extent to which agriculture can contribute to the production of rubber, which to-day is an essential war product.
A few nights ago the hon. member for Parry Sound gave us some facts regarding the production of rubber from grain alcohol. I believe it is a well-known fact to-day that much of Russia's rubber supply comes from potato alcohol. I was surprised this afternoon to hear the minister express fears that we in this country may have a surplus of potatoes in the fall. There is abundant evidence to show that grain alcohol can be used for the production of rubber in half the time and apparently at approximately half the cost of synthetic rubber made from petroleum. A report of the United States senate committee on agriculture gives figures from which I deduce that our present carryover of wheat is sufficient to provide all the rubber that is necessary to supply the military needs of both the United States and Canada. These figures are given by a committee of the United States senate exploring ways and means of assisting agriculture. Furthermore, it is a well known fact that there are at least four commercial plants operating in the United States to-day making synthetic rubber from milkweed. There are at Akron three commercial plants actually producing rubber and supplying it to the United States military forces-rubber that is made from the latex produced by milkweed. There is also, I understand, a factory in California. There is also available at the present time a fairly large supply of milkweed seeds and plants for the production and growing of milkweed on a
commercial basis. What heretofore has been known as a weed can now be grown in about five or six months on arid land where there are two or three inches of soil. It can be grown very cheaply, and rubber can be produced from that plant at a price much lower than that of the product obtained from either petroleum or the para tree. Has the minister investigated the possibility of opening up a new source of revenue for our agriculturists, giving us an industry that, when the war is over, will keep the production of synthetic rubber out of the hands of the great oil monopolies which exist at the present time?

This afternoon the hon.
member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) and the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Fulford) stressed the fact that in their districts a number of sales were being held at which valuable dairy stock were being disposed of, and a large percentage of that stock was finding its way into the slaughter houses and being exported. I think the majority of western members can duplicate that statement. Last year I attended many sales at which valuable stock was sold and dragged away to the slaughter houses. I believe, as one member stated, that this could be very largely overcome if a higher price were paid for butterfat. The same applies to poultry. We are given to understand that there is an urgent need for a greater production of eggs, and yet I received word1 the other day that the price received for eggs was around 10 cents a dozen on the average. We cannot expect the farmer to be enthusiastic about keeping poultry in the month of March when he gets only 10 cents a dtozen for his eggs. Last fall I saw pullets and yearlings being shipped to the packing plants. The hon. member for Fraser Valley emphasized the fact that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was not to blame for the present standard of agricultural prices. The hon. member blamed the wartime prices and trade board, and I shall discuss this matter at greater length when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is before the committee. The question I wish to ask the Minister of Agriculture is this. Surely when the wartime prices and trade board set a ceiling on agricultural prices they consulted the minister and his department, or are we to understand that the wartime prices and trade board set this level of prices against the recommendation of the Department of Agriculture? In other words, is the. Minister of Agriculture himself opposed to the price of agricultural products being held to the present level?
